title: French Defense: tactics and traps
outcomes: Explains how a check that opens a line wins a queen after a greedy capture, and when the same idea fails
Names the ingredients of the h7 bishop sacrifice and checks them before playing it
Finds a defence to the h7 threat in a Winawer position (a pawn or knight on the d3-h7 diagonal, or a guard of g5) and says why each works
Asks before every capture what it allows with check

steps.text: **What this lesson trains.** A trap is a move that looks natural and loses to one exact reply. This lesson has two patterns worth checking: a grab that opens a line with check, and the bishop sacrifice on h7. You will see each, learn the conditions it needs, and meet a look-alike where it fails. Engine claims use depth 16 [V].
steps.chapter: Trap 1: the check that opens a line

steps.caption: The Advance Variation after 5...Qb6. White to move.

line.say: White develops the bishop, which will look toward h7.
Black takes the centre pawn and opens the diagonal for the queen.
White recaptures and rebuilds the chain.
Black takes a second pawn. This already loses a knight for a pawn: White is about three pawns or more ahead whatever Black plays next (depth 16).
White recaptures; the knight on d4 is attacked by the queen.

claims.statement: After 8.Nxd4 the knight on d4 is attacked and no white piece defends it.
The bishop on d3 stands between the queen and d4, so d4 has no white defender.
After 8.Nxd4 the engine rates White at least three pawns ahead, whatever Black plays next (depth 16).

steps.prompt: The queen can take a knight that nothing guards. Write what you would check before capturing.

steps.caption: Black has taken: the queen is on d4. White to move.

line.say: The bishop moves with check and, in the same move, opens the d-file for the queen.
Black must answer the check, so the bishop interposes.
White trades off the blocker, again with check.
The king recaptures, and the queen is still on d4.
The white queen takes the black queen: White is a queen up.

claims.statement: Bb5+ is the engine's best move (depth 16).
After Bb5+ and Black's best defence White is at least six pawns up in counting value.

steps.text: **The pattern and its conditions.** A move that gives check and uncovers an attack at once wins because the opponent can answer only one of the two. It needs a blocker of your own on the line, a blocker that can step off with a real check, and a check your opponent cannot meet by taking your queen or trading queens first. Before you capture, ask what the capture lets your opponent do *with check*.

steps.text: [H] **Why such captures look safe.** A player counts attackers and defenders of the square first. Here the defender, the white queen, is hidden behind its own bishop, so the count says one attacker and no defender. The data we hold cannot test what players think; it holds results. Do you agree?

steps.text: **The bishop sacrifice on h7.** The bishop takes on h7 with check and the king must take. If a knight can then check from g5, the queen arrives on h5 and the king has no safe square. [H] In the Winawer Black may castle early, which puts the king in front of White's queen, bishop and knight. The next board builds the setup one move at a time.
steps.chapter: Trap 2: the bishop sacrifice on h7

steps.caption: The Winawer after 6...c5 (1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e5 Ne7 5.a3 Bxc3+ 6.bxc3 c5). White to move.

line.say: The queen attacks g7 and aims at the kingside.
Black castles, putting the king beside the pieces that point at it.
The knight heads for g5, where it will attack h7 and f7.
Black develops the knight and adds pressure on d4.
The bishop aims straight at h7, which only the king guards.

claims.statement: Only the king, on g8, defends h7.
After 9.Bd3 the bishop attacks the long diagonal as far as h7.

steps.caption: Black has played the quiet 9...a6. White to move.

line.say: The bishop takes with check.
The king must take; no other piece can.
The knight checks; the other king squares lose to mate, so Black goes back.
The king returns to g8.
The queen threatens Qh7 mate.
Black makes room for the king.
The queen takes with check.
The king steps to f8, the only square.
The queen checks again.
Black blocks with the knight.

claims.statement: Bxh7+ is the engine's best move (depth 16).
After Bxh7+ the engine rates White at least four pawns ahead (depth 16).

steps.text: **The ingredients.** [I] The sacrifice works when the bishop sees h7 along a clear diagonal, a knight can check from g5 and nothing covers g5, only the king guards h7, and the king has no safe flight. Remove one and it usually fails. Black has two ways to do that: put a pawn or knight on the diagonal, or cover g5 with ...f6. A white pawn on e5 keeps a black knight off f6, the usual guard.

The king takes the bishop.

Bxh7+ is at least 300 cp worse than the best move here (depth 16).

steps.text: **What the numbers say.** [V] Our top-level tree (329,379 games, both players 2,500 or more, up to 24 plies) holds 231 positions with White to move, a bishop on d3, a black king on g8, black pawns on e6, d5 and h7, and Bxh7+ legal. At depth 12 the engine never rated it above minus 0.64 pawns. [I] In the master games we hold it never worked, so masters do not leave the guard out: it punishes a missing guard and is no default.

[H] **Why masters rarely allow it.** Strong players seem to check the diagonal to h7 and the square g5 before a quiet move. The French habit of ...f6 and ...f5 may partly answer these ideas. Our data counts positions, not thoughts, so this is a hypothesis.

steps.prompt: Where in your own games will you check a bishop aimed at h7 before you play a quiet move?

steps.text:
**Recap: what to remember.**
- Before a capture, ask what it allows with check.
- A bishop in front of its queen can open a line with a check.
- The h7 sacrifice needs a clear diagonal, an uncovered g5, and no safe square for the king.
- Defend with a pawn or knight on the diagonal, or cover g5 with ...f6.
- A pinned pawn cannot recapture: that is why Bxh6 can work.
